concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality (AR) is an enhanced version of reality created by technology, in which computer-generated digital content is overlaid on the real world in real time and registered in 3D, so the user perceives and interacts with the enhanced environment.

defining_facts.text: Augmented reality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state in which the real environment is augmented with virtual content.
Augmented virtuality on the reality-virtuality continuum is the intermediate state, opposite augmented reality, in which the virtual environment is augmented with real-world content.
Augmented reality (AR), unlike virtual reality (VR), does not require an immersive experience and instead emphasizes augmenting real-world content with digital content.
Augmented reality (AR) applications include archaeology, architecture, industrial manufacturing, commerce (particularly e-commerce), gaming, and medical domains, among other domains.
In archaeology, augmented reality (AR) can display things that are not visible to the naked eye on a screen and can reconstruct lost structures.
In industrial manufacturing, augmented reality (AR) can allow a person to see things while repairing or troubleshooting a component of an industrial setup.
The presence of many augmented reality (AR) applications in commerce, particularly e-commerce, is one motivation for the metaverse concept.
Pokemon Go is a famous augmented reality (AR) gaming application.

Augmented reality (AR) is defined by the Merriam-Webster dictionary as an enhanced version of reality created by the use of technology, primarily computer technology, to overlay digital information on an image of something being viewed through a device.

The systemic definition of augmented reality (AR) states that an AR system should have three characteristics: combining the real world with virtual content, being interactive in real time so that interaction with the digital content added to the real-world view is reflected immediately, and being registered in 3D.

An augmented reality (AR) system has four characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content such as image, video, or text; the enhancement is registered in 3D so that it appears at its appropriate place rather than randomly and mixes seamlessly with real-world objects; the enhancement is experienced through the user's sensory organs; and the system supports the user's interaction with the digital content in the enhanced environment rather than separately, giving the user the feel of being in reality at all times.

A system is identified as an augmented reality (AR) system by checking the four AR characteristics one by one, and it is an AR system only if all four are satisfied; if at least one characteristic is not satisfied, it is not an AR system.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.
An augmented reality (AR) system can superimpose extra information, such as non-existent furniture, as digital content over the real-world view of a room.

The dictionary definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a medium consisting of immersive computer-generated environments in which elements of physical and virtual environments are combined, but this definition is not categorical about how MR differs from virtual reality (VR) or augmented reality (AR).

One definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR comprises everything in between the two extremes of the reality-virtuality continuum, the real environment and the virtual environment, so augmented reality (AR) is included in this broader definition of MR.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) is that MR denotes the capability to combine augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR) technologies in the same application or on the same device, so such a combined application is called MR from a developer's point of view.

Another definition of mixed reality (MR) describes MR as a strong version of augmented reality (AR), meaning a more capable version of augmented reality that has an advanced understanding of the physical environment and may be bound to specific hardware.

In one definition used by many people, mixed reality (MR) is a synonym for augmented reality (AR), because in both cases the user views reality augmented or enhanced with digital content overlaid on the view of reality, and can interact with that content.

Because most definitions of mixed reality (MR) are confusing and the controversy is not needed for this course, the course assumes that MR is the same technology as augmented reality (AR) and treats the two terms as interchangeable.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real, because a person cannot distinguish the experienced environment from their real environment and perceives it as that real environment.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: metaverse
concepts.definition: Metaverse is a broad view of an all-around three-dimensional environment in which people act as in the real world through natural interaction with digital content, reimagining human interaction with the digital world rather than being merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology.

defining_facts.text: The metaverse is a term that has been in use for more than 30 years and has heavily stimulated growth in the extended reality field.

The metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology, while one broad view is that it reimagines the way humans interact with the digital world.

In the metaverse, people act as they do in the real world in an all-around three-dimensional environment and use natural interaction with digital content, unlike current mostly flat two-dimensional screen interactions with occasional three-dimensional interaction.

The metaverse is not yet fully realized because current technology is not advanced enough and has technological bottlenecks, but companies are investing heavily to make it a reality, with growth potential in both hardware and software.

concepts.name: non-immersive virtual reality system
concepts.definition: A Non-immersive virtual reality system is a limited class of computer application that provides a computer-generated environment in which a user controls characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment. The user is psychologically engaged and remains physically attached to the real world, while the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

defining_facts.text: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) system is a specific, limited class of computer application, not any computer application, that provides a computer-generated environment in which the user can control characters or activities while retaining control of the physical environment, and the virtual environment does not directly interact with the user.

A non-immersive virtual reality (VR) application is a regular computer system or software that completely takes away the user's attention, so the user is psychologically engaged and may not experience the real world, although the user's eyes, ears, and other sensory organs remain open and the user is physically attached to the real world.

Non-immersive virtual reality (VR) includes specifically gaming applications, such as games on PlayStation, Xbox, or similar systems and games like World of Warcraft or similar games, that rely on computer or video game console displays and input devices such as keyboards, mice, and handheld controllers.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

concepts.name: semi-immersive virtual reality system
concepts.definition: Semi-immersive virtual reality system is a type of virtual reality system, positioned between non-immersive and fully immersive systems, that gives the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

defining_facts.text: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) is in between non-immersive and fully immersive VR, giving the user a partial immersive experience by blocking some but not all senses; for example, the eyes may be blocked while ears and skin remain exposed to real-world signals.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) can be a three-dimensional virtual environment in which users can move by themselves through a computer screen, a VR box, or a VR headset, with a VR headset being the common example; users typically have no real physical movements, and examples include virtual tours using only a headset, which can be device-based or web-based.

Semi-immersive virtual reality (VR) systems are the most cost-effective and commonly used form of VR, and most commercial immersive applications are semi-immersive because they give partial immersion while leaving the user free to sense the real world.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

concepts.name: fully immersive virtual reality system
concepts.definition: Fully immersive virtual reality system is a virtual reality system that completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the virtual world and feels physically present in it.

defining_facts.text: From a systems point of view, virtual reality (VR) systems are broadly categorized into non-immersive, semi-immersive, and fully immersive systems because market applications offer varying degrees of immersion rather than all being fully immersive.

A fully immersive virtual reality (VR) system completely blocks the user's ability to sense the real world by blocking all senses, so the user senses only the things happening in the virtual world, feels physically present in it, and has the user's sense of reality replaced by virtual realism.

Fully immersive virtual reality (VR) systems, such as dedicated virtual shooting game zones, use many devices such as helmets, gloves, body connectors with sense detectors, and body suits, so users view the virtual environment through a helmet or head-mounted display and their actual movements, such as running, jumping, crouching, shooting, and throwing, their reactions, and even a blink of an eye are detected and translated into actions in the virtual world while the user cannot sense anything in the real world.

Among virtual reality (VR) systems, fully immersive systems are the costliest and commercially rare because they are difficult to afford, while semi-immersive and non-immersive systems are more common.

never_defined.name: application domain
never_defined.definition: An application domain is an area in which virtual reality or augmented reality applications are used.

never_defined.name: screen
never_defined.definition: A screen is a display on which an image or content is shown so that a human can perceive it.

never_defined.name: beacon
never_defined.definition: A beacon is used by a passenger app at points in a terminal to tell a passenger their exact location and the direction to move to reach a desired terminal.

never_defined.name: mobile phone
never_defined.definition: A mobile phone is used for augmented reality applications, and early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones but were still used for mobile-based augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: augmented reality application
never_defined.definition: An Augmented reality application is an application that emphasizes augmenting digital content onto the real-world view rather than being immersive.

never_defined.name: medical training
never_defined.definition: Medical training is one of the augmented reality applications in healthcare.

never_defined.name: telemedicine
never_defined.definition: Telemedicine is an augmented reality application in healthcare that enables medical professionals to interact with patients.

never_defined.name: diagnosis
never_defined.definition: Diagnosis is a medical activity that real-time information in treatment areas of augmented reality applications supports.

never_defined.name: surgery
never_defined.definition: Surgery is one of the things in treatment areas that augmented reality applications can support with real-time information.

never_defined.name: treatment plan
never_defined.definition: A treatment plan is one of the things supported by real-time information in treatment areas in healthcare augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: vein network
never_defined.definition: Vein network is a patient's internal vein network that can be scanned and visualized by an augmented reality device pointed at the skin surface to help decide the treatment course.

never_defined.name: quick response code
never_defined.definition: A quick response code (QR) is a marker used in marker-based augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: simple color code
never_defined.definition: A simple color code is a marker used in marker-based augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: color bar
never_defined.definition: A Color bar is one of the markers used in marker-based augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: fiducial marker
never_defined.definition: A fiducial marker is a marker used in marker-based augmented reality applications and camera-based full-body tracking, and can aid registration.

never_defined.name: computer vision
never_defined.definition: Computer vision (CV) is an enabling technology for augmented reality and mixed reality applications that detects, recognizes, and tracks objects in real-world scenes.

never_defined.name: location sensor
never_defined.definition: A location sensor is a sensor that detects a user's location with respect to a reference frame in location-based markerless augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: reference frame
never_defined.definition: A reference frame is a coordinate system in which locations or positions are defined.

never_defined.name: light projector
never_defined.definition: A light projector is a projector used in projection-based markerless augmented reality applications to project digital content onto an object, a surface, or a space.

never_defined.name: holographic projection
never_defined.definition: Holographic projection is a projection-based technique that can be used in augmented reality application development.

never_defined.name: object recognition
never_defined.definition: Object recognition is a computer vision operation used in outlining-based markerless augmented reality applications to recreate a user's immediate surroundings and digitally enhance the view.

never_defined.name: marker-based augmented reality
never_defined.definition: Marker-based augmented reality is a type of augmented reality system that recognizes a marker image by matching its color, shape, and size, and displays a three-dimensional model in the marker's place.

never_defined.name: markerless augmented reality
never_defined.definition: Markerless augmented reality is a type of augmented reality system and one of the main technologies relied on by handheld augmented reality devices.

never_defined.name: computer vision-based augmented reality application
never_defined.definition: A computer vision-based augmented reality application is an augmented reality application that is superimposition-based or outline-based.

never_defined.name: superimposition-based application
never_defined.definition: A superimposition-based application is a kind of computer vision-based augmented reality application.

never_defined.name: outline-based application
never_defined.definition: An outline-based application is a kind of computer vision-based augmented reality (AR) application.

never_defined.name: projection-based technique
never_defined.definition: A projection-based technique is a technique that can be used in augmented reality application development.

never_defined.name: virtual reality application
never_defined.definition: A Virtual reality application is an immersive application that involves creating a virtual environment, rendering a stereoscopic output view, and incorporating interactions.
